opus-5.5.text:
I think it matters a lot, and for a few reasons.

First, when you rely on an off-the-shelf encoder, you inherit all of its choices: the data it was trained on, the languages it covers well or badly, the way it compresses the signal. For a lot of applications that's fine, but if you want a model that really understands speech, not just transcribes it, you want control over that whole pipeline. Things like tone, hesitation, who is speaking, background context: a lot of that information gets thrown away if the encoder was only optimized for transcription.

Second, it's about how the encoder fits with the language model. When you train both together, or at least design them together, you can make the representations line up much better with what the LLM expects. You get better efficiency in terms of tokens per second of audio, better latency, and the model reasons over the audio more naturally instead of treating it as a noisy text input.

Third, there's the multilingual side, which has always been important for us. Many existing speech systems are very strong in English and then degrade quickly for other languages, accents, or dialects. If we want our models to work well for customers across Europe and elsewhere, we need to own the data and training decisions to fix that.

And finally, a lot of our customers deploy on-premise or at the edge, so having small, efficient encoders we fully control and can optimize is really valuable. It's the same philosophy as for text: if you build the core components yourself, you understand them deeply, you can iterate quickly, and you're not limited by someone else's roadmap.

r001.rationale: The response notes that existing speech systems often underperform across languages and accents, but it does not identify a causal audio encoder or say that Mistral is addressing a lack of such encoders available to the community.

r002.rationale: The response discusses tradeoffs of off-the-shelf encoders generally, but does not mention Whisper or explain how experience using its encoder changed design considerations.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: So the honest answer is that for a long time we didn't want to do it. Our view at Mistral was always: focus on the thing that matters most, which is the core language model, and don't spread yourself across ten modalities when you have a small team. For audio, we actually started with the pragmatic approach, which is to take an existing encoder, something like a Whisper-style model, and plug it into our LLM. And that gets you pretty far, frankly. You can get a decent speech model in a few weeks that way.

But you hit a ceiling fairly quickly, and the ceiling is not really about accuracy on a transcription benchmark. It's about what the encoder throws away. An encoder trained purely for ASR learns to be a very good text extractor, and in doing so it discards everything that is not text: who is speaking, tone, hesitations, background, the fact that there are two people talking over each other, the language switch in the middle of a sentence. And then you're asking the language model to reason about a conversation using a representation that already deleted half of the conversation. That's a bad starting point if what you want is not a transcription tool but a model that actually understands speech.

The other thing is control. When you depend on someone else's encoder, you inherit their tokenization, their frame rate, their language coverage, their biases, and you can't fix any of it. We care a lot about European languages, about code-switching, about low-resource languages, and those are precisely the places where off-the-shelf encoders are weakest. Training our own means we decide what goes in the data, what the model is optimized for, and crucially we can train the encoder jointly, or at least in a way that is aligned with how the LLM is going to consume it. That joint training is where most of the quality comes from. The encoder and the decoder shouldn't be two strangers glued together with an adapter.

And then there is the efficiency argument, which people underestimate. If you want real-time voice, latency is everything. A general-purpose encoder produces a lot of tokens per second of audio, and that is expensive to feed into the model and it slows everything down. If you own the encoder you can compress aggressively, you can tune the token rate to what the language model actually needs, and that is what makes a low-latency product feasible rather than a demo.

So I'd say the value is less about "we have our own encoder" as a bragging right and more that audio stops being a bolt-on. It becomes a native input, the same way text is. And once you're there, the next step, generating speech, doing real conversational agents, becomes much more natural. We're still small compared to the big labs, so we pick our battles, but this was one we concluded we couldn't outsource.

r002.rationale: It contrasts using a Whisper-style encoder with building in-house, explaining that reliance on an external encoder brings inherited tokenization, frame rate, language coverage, and biases, while in-house development enables aligned training and control over those choices.

astra-6.text:
I think the main value is having control over the whole system. If you take an existing audio encoder and freeze it, you inherit its strengths, but also its limitations. Developing our own lets us train it together with the language model and optimize for the things we care about, like latency, multilingual understanding, and robustness to noise.

And audio contains much more than a transcript. There’s intonation, emotion, the way people take turns speaking. If you convert everything to text first, you lose some of that information. So the interesting opportunity is to build a model that can use the audio directly, rather than treating speech as just another way to type a prompt.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main value is being able to train the whole system together. If you take an audio encoder that was developed separately and connect it to a language model, you inherit a lot of choices about what information it preserves. For transcription, that may be fine. But if you want the model to understand tone, handle interruptions, or have a natural conversation, you may want a different representation.

Developing the encoder ourselves gives us control over those trade-offs, including latency and compute. It also lets us improve the audio side as we improve the language model. The goal is to make audio a native capability, so the model can use what it hears beyond just the words.
